newsitem.title: USA: SENATE DEMOCRATS - Budget amendment would lock up economy.
newsitem.headline: SENATE DEMOCRATS - Budget amendment would lock up economy.

text.p: Senate Democrats argued Monday that the government should be permitted to run a deficit when the economy turns sour as a way to protect the country from sliding into depression.

Illinois Sen. Richard Durbin said the balanced budget amendment to the Constitution proposed by Republicans, which would require the government balance its books every year, was too restrictive during times of disaster or economic emergency.

Final passage of the constitutional amendment will be extremely close in both the House and Senate. If it passes later this month by a two-thirds vote in both houses, it must be ratified by 38 of 50 state legislatures, a process that could take seven years.

Durbin's amendment would require only a simple majority to approve deficit spending, not the "super majority" three-fifths vote required under the Republicans' budget amendment. The amendment would also require a three-fifths vote to borrow money and would make it harder to raise taxes.
The proposal is only one of several controversial changes to the balanced budget amendment which Democrats hoped to use to erode support for the budget amendment.
"Let's not be in a situation where we handcuff the American economy ... That just makes common sense," said Sen. Kent Conrad, Democrat of North Dakota.

Supporting their cause were more than 1,000 economists who said it could prevent the government from using economic stabilisers -- unemployment payments, federal spending and tax cuts -- to keep recessions from moving into depressions.

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch replied that Congress would act if necessary. "If we have a true economic emergency we will get the three-fifths vote. If it isn't, if it doesn't measure up, the three-fifths vote won't be granted," the Utah Republican said.

In the House, the Judiciary Committee for the second time called off its vote on the amendment. Democrats said it was because Republicans were divided on whether Social Security Trust Funds should be used to balance the budget.

The Social Security issue poses the biggest threat to passage of the constitutional amendment. While Republicans have all 55 of their members and seven Democrats on board, they are within one or two of reaching the magic 67 votes for passage.

In the House, the final vote had been originally scheduled for Feb. 26, but the Judiciary panel's delay could force a Senate vote first -- a boost for the cause among wavering House lawmakers if it passes.
In 1995, the amendment passed the House but went down by one vote in the Senate. Election year changes in 1996 gave it bore support in the Senate and cost it votes in the House.

President Clinton and several Democrats have pressed to take Social Security funds out of the budget, on the argument that including them in the budget makes it difficult to keep the fund solvent in the next century when the baby-boom generation retires.
